video_title: Ukraine War: Putin, Zelenskyy, Trump, Drones and the Future of Warfare | Lex Fridman Podcast #504
gist: Michael Kofman and Preston Stewart argue 2026 is Ukraine's best year on the ground since 2023 while Russia's infiltration-heavy approach has hit diminishing returns, pushing Moscow toward strategic bombardment of Ukrainian infrastructure. They detail drone-war economics (8-10k FPVs per day per side, 30-40 drones per tank kill), Russian data falsification, Russia's 44%-of-budget war spending, and why they see no near-term peace, with ceasefire risks and a weak US policy stance.

insights.claim: Michael Kofman judges 2026 as Ukraine's best year of ground combat performance since roughly the summer 2023 offensive, and Russia's worst since winter 2023, with the inflection point around summer-fall 2025.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Consensus 'grinding Russian advance' narrative is stale; watch for repricing of war-outcome and ceasefire-leverage assumptions in European defense and reconstruction plays.
insights.quote: this year for Ukraine is the best year of combat performance for them on the ground since probably about the summer of twenty twenty-three offensive

insights.claim: Russia's ground approach of grinding infantry infiltration has hit diminishing returns since about summer 2025, and Russia is shifting weight to strategic bombardment, which historically rarely achieves maximalist political aims when the ground campaign is floundering.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Expect continued escalation of strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure rather than ground breakthroughs; infrastructure/energy rebuild demand keeps rising.
insights.quote: strategic bombardment does not have a great track record or even a good track record of achieving maximalist political aims in the war

insights.claim: Ukraine is running two localized offensives in 2026 (an air-assault grouping in Zaporizhzhia and Third Corps operation 'Vihod' near Liman) that have liberated territory and wiped out Russian 2025 gains, in some cases gaining more terrain than the much larger summer 2023 offensive.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: The front is more fluid than a 'positional stalemate' framing suggests; map-based narratives lag reality.

insights.claim: The front is a vast gray zone roughly 15 km forward and back of the line, held by sparse three-man pickets several hundred meters apart backed by drones, minefields and artillery rather than cohesive defensive lines.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Low-density, drone-dependent defense is the template militaries will copy, shifting procurement from mass manpower to sensors, drones and mines.

insights.claim: Drones inflict roughly 80% of losses, but Kofman argues they only work as part of a combined system with minefields and artillery, which remains essential in poor spring/fall weather when drones degrade.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Artillery shell demand does not disappear in a drone age; balanced exposure across munitions and drones is warranted.
insights.quote: the statistics out there do show that drones inflict 80% of the losses. However, it is really a combination of things

insights.claim: Kofman frames the question of who is 'winning' as a debate over whether Ukraine's 2026 advantage is a lasting secular trend or merely a window of opportunity, cautioning that advantages like Russia's in 2024-25 can reverse.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Avoid extrapolating current battlefield momentum linearly into ceasefire timing or reconstruction trades.
insights.quote: is that going to be a lasting advantage, is that a secular trend, or is that a window of opportunity for Ukraine?

insights.claim: Neither Russia nor Ukraine appears near collapse; analysts repeatedly predicted Ukraine's imminent collapse and were wrong, and the current mode of fighting is not conducive to generating decisive momentum.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Tail-risk of sudden collapse is low on both sides; price a prolonged war base case.

insights.claim: One side alone uses roughly 8,000-10,000 FPV drones per day, i.e. hundreds of thousands per month, exceeding all personnel and equipment on the battlefield by a large margin.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Signals enormous consumable-drone demand; a structural volume market for low-cost drone makers, batteries, optics and components.
insights.quote: I'd say for FPVs, it's probably somewhere eight to 10,000 per day, just those, not including other types of tactical drones.

insights.claim: Drone kill ratios are far worse than videos imply: about 5 drones per soldier, 15-20 for an infantry fighting vehicle, 30-40 for a tank, and in one extreme case 79 for a heavily protected Russian tank.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Per-target drone costs are an order of magnitude higher than the '$500 drone kills a tank' narrative; model unit demand accordingly.

insights.claim: A drone-supported Ukrainian mechanized company now expects to absorb close to 300 drone hits during an assault, meaning vehicle survivability against FPVs is a core design requirement.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Demand for vehicle protection, EW and counter-drone kits on armored platforms should rise.
insights.quote: a company that, mechanized company that goes on the attack now expects to take about close to 300 hits in that assault

insights.claim: Autonomy and AI in this war are over-hyped: almost all systems are remotely piloted, typically requiring two to three people per drone team, with semi-autonomy limited mostly to terminal guidance.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of defense-AI valuations premised on battlefield autonomy already being proven; manpower, training and maintenance still dominate.
insights.quote: to some extent it's been over-hyped in terms of the percentages being, the percentage of the fight that's actually being run that way

insights.claim: Fiber-optic tethered drones, popularized by Russia around Kursk, are immune to jamming and undetectable by analog signal receivers, now reach roughly 50 km, but remain about 15% or less of tactical strike drones.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart and Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Erodes the value of pure RF-jamming EW; favors physical/kinetic counter-drone and fiber/spool supply chains.

insights.claim: The technology-and-tactics cycle between Russia and Ukraine runs about three to four months: Ukraine innovates bottom-up faster via unit-level 'defense startups', while Russia is slower but better at scaling a proven solution across the force.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Defense products have very short obsolescence windows; favor agile, iterative suppliers over long-cycle programs.
insights.quote: there's been about a three to four-month cycle of evolution of technology and tactics in this war

insights.claim: Russia and Ukraine have shifted from few expensive drones to masses of low-cost, near-attritable systems, contrasted with US Predator/Reaper-class platforms costing $20M+.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that procurement shifts toward cheap, mass-produced systems, pressuring exquisite-platform incumbents.

insights.claim: Russia's strike campaign has shifted from cruise and ballistic missiles to saturation attacks by one-way attack drones, which have evolved from slow propeller types to jet-powered models that are effectively light ground-launched cruise missiles.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Raises demand for interceptors and layered air defense in Ukraine and across Europe.

insights.claim: Ukrainian CODE 9.2 regiment used a SkyFall drone carrying an evacuation pod to fly a wounded soldier out from about 30 km away, showing robotics now extend into casualty evacuation.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Military robotics use cases are broadening beyond strike to logistics and medevac.

insights.claim: The US military is still figuring out drone ownership and doctrine, and is using a 'drone dominance' program to find small agile manufacturers to catch up.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Opportunity for small US drone makers to win Pentagon contracts as the military plays catch-up.
insights.quote: There's a drone dominance program right now that the military is spearheading, trying to identify small manufacturers that can be agile

themes.theme: Russian infiltration tactics and command dysfunction

insights.claim: Russia now mainly advances through small infantry infiltration and motorcycle/ATV light motorized assaults, accepting extreme losses; a US volunteer described it as workable only if you are willing to lose 90-95% of your men.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Russian advances come at unsustainable manpower cost, reinforcing the diminishing-returns thesis.
insights.quote: You're just gonna lose 90, 95% of your guys along the way.

insights.claim: Russian maps consistently claim positions roughly 10-15 km beyond what forces actually hold, and this falsification feeds up to Putin, distorting his view that Russia is still advancing in the Donbas.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Kremlin negotiation posture may rest on false battlefield data, making a near-term compromise less likely.
insights.quote: on the Russian maps, they consistently claim themselves to be something like 15 kilometers, 10 kilometers at least forward of where they actually are

insights.claim: Russian offensives typically intensify in October-November with casualties rising because commanders are pressed to actually seize territory they previously claimed in reports.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: A seasonal pattern to watch for Q4 escalation in fighting intensity.

insights.claim: After Wagner's dismantling the Russian military 'Wagnerized', copying convict assault units (Shtorm-Z, Shtorm-V), which brought some success but overspecialized it in small-unit assaults and eroded its ability to run large complex operations.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Russia's force structure is now poorly suited to large-scale breakthrough operations, lowering the odds of a sudden Russian operational win.

insights.claim: Russia's coercive, centralized, low-trust military culture creates a garbage-in, garbage-out planning problem, whereas Ukraine's Western-style delegated authority drives faster bottom-up adaptation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman and Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Culture and decision rights, not just hardware counts, determine military effectiveness; relevant to judging adversary capability claims.

insights.claim: Prigozhin's 2023 mutiny never had a real chance of regime change because personalist authoritarian regimes eliminate alternatives, and Prigozhin was used as leverage to negotiate amnesty before being killed in a demonstrative plane explosion.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Discount scenarios of Kremlin elite rupture as a war-ending catalyst.
insights.quote: In personalist authoritarian regimes- The first thing they do is eliminate alternatives.

insights.claim: Bakhmut Syndrome describes defending a symbolic city past the point it makes military sense; Russia took a year to move from Bakhmut to neighboring Chasiv Yar, showing the city's loss was not decisive, and Kostiantynivka now risks a similar pattern.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman and Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Headlines about symbolic city falls are poor indicators of war trajectory.

themes.theme: War economies, manpower and external support

insights.claim: Russia spends about 44% of its government budget and roughly 9-10% of GDP on the war, and key Russian economic elites began saying publicly in spring that this level of spending is not sustainable.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Rising fiscal strain on Russia; watch ruble, budget deficits and energy revenue for pressure toward negotiation.
insights.quote: Russia's spending forty-four percent of the government budget on the war, and maybe somewhere around nine to ten percent of GDP.

insights.claim: Because so much spending goes into military production that is not economically valuable, the Russian economy is slowly consuming itself, yet it still has resources to fight into 2027.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Base case is a war lasting into 2027; Russian economic deterioration is gradual rather than a near-term trigger.
insights.quote: the economy is slowly consuming itself

insights.claim: Preston Stewart admits Western sanctions did far less damage than he and many others expected because Russia found many workarounds, and public frustration over living standards has not materialized.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Sanctions alone are an unreliable catalyst for ending the war; don't overweight sanction-driven collapse scenarios.
insights.quote: I thought that the sanctions would have done a lot more damage. At this point, I think a lot of people did, and it just hasn't.

insights.claim: Russia is suffering 30,000-plus casualties a month and has begun a coercive 'shadow mobilization' as some regions struggle to meet recruitment targets.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Manpower stress is a slow-burning constraint; a formal mobilization would be a major signal to watch.

insights.claim: Russia relies heavily on China for machine tools and components, and at one point North Korea supplied about 40% of Russia's artillery ammunition and sent troops to fight in Kursk.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Secondary-sanction and export-control risk around Chinese suppliers of dual-use goods persists.
insights.quote: at one point in the war, North Korea was providing 40% of Russian artillery ammunition

insights.claim: Ukraine's strategy includes striking Russian energy exports, refining capacity and now data centers to erode the Russian state's revenue, alongside air defense and holding the front.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Ongoing supply risk for Russian refined product exports; relevant to diesel/refining margins.

insights.claim: The US no longer gives direct financial aid but still supplies considerable equipment, munitions and intelligence via foreign military sales paid for by Europeans.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: European-funded FMS sustains US defense contractor revenue tied to Ukraine regardless of US aid politics.
insights.quote: Just Europeans are paying for it, okay?

insights.claim: Europeans are likely to come up with more funding for Ukraine next year if needed, so both sides can sustain the war into 2027.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Supports continued European defense and Ukraine-related budget growth.

themes.theme: Negotiations, US policy and ceasefire risk

insights.claim: Kofman is pessimistic on near-term peace: Putin likely waits to see whether the winter strike campaign weakens Ukraine's bargaining position and whether spring European elections such as France's shift conditions in Russia's favor.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: France's spring election is a key event risk for Ukraine-support policy and European defense sentiment.

insights.claim: The most plausible near-term deals are partial, compartmentalized ceasefires, such as halting energy-infrastructure strikes or strikes on Black Sea shipping, which escalated this year.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: A Black Sea shipping ceasefire would ease freight/insurance risk and grain/energy flows; watch for it.

insights.claim: Russia's war aims remain far beyond its military means, including the rest of Donbas plus caps on Ukraine's army and NATO orientation, while Ukraine has narrowed its demands to a ceasefire on the line of control.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: The gap between demands and battlefield reality implies no imminent settlement.

insights.claim: A ceasefire without real security guarantees risks becoming a rearmament pause, leaving Ukraine vulnerable 6-8 months later after demobilization, as happened after Minsk I and II.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: A signed ceasefire is not equal to durable peace; reconstruction investors should price renewed-war risk.
insights.quote: ceasefires can often just become rearmament periods to renew hostilities

insights.claim: Both guests judge the Trump administration's Ukraine policy as largely ineffective: it gave up US leverage by repositioning as a neutral arbiter, applied little sanctions pressure on Russia, and has been distracted by the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Preston Stewart and Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: US policy remains capricious; expect headline-driven volatility around peace talks rather than a clean resolution.

insights.claim: The US war with Iran had a material and political impact on the Ukraine war, and Ukraine offered to help the US with interceptors, creating an opening for joint production deals that Preston Stewart says the US has left on the table.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman and Preston Stewart
insights.so_what: Interceptor production capacity is a shared bottleneck; joint US-Ukraine production would be a notable defense-industrial development.

insights.claim: Kofman credits the Trump administration with one positive: forcing parties to articulate end-of-war requirements, since the Biden administration and Europeans never had a real plan to end the war.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Peace process scaffolding now exists, even if progress is fitful.
insights.quote: As long as it takes is a slogan, not a plan.

insights.claim: Kofman argues the US is advantaged by its ability to scale complex combined-arms operations, but it is uncertain whether those advantages hold in a war featuring mass drones, and Russia plans to fight this way in the future.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman
insights.so_what: Supports sustained Western spending on counter-drone, drone, and doctrine adaptation.
insights.quote: The future's already here. It's not evenly distributed
